title: Conditional diffusion for single-cell Hi-C data imputation and enhancement with scHiC-Diff.
authors: Liu, Wuhao; Fang, Zhaoyu; Du, Xuyan; Tang, Li; Li, Min
abstract: Single-cell high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (scHi-C) enables the analysis of cell-to-cell variability in three-dimensional (3D) genome organization, but its utility is severely limited by pervasive technical dropouts, leading to extremely sparse contact maps. Accurately identifying dropout events and imputing the corresponding missing chromatin contacts remains a challenging problem, as technical dropouts are confounded with genuine absences of chromatin interactions. Existing imputation and enhancement methods often rely on smoothing strategies or restrictive parametric likelihood assumptions, which may obscure fine-scale chromatin structures and cell-specific features. Here, we present scHiC-Diff, a conditional diffusion-based framework for scHi-C data imputation and enhancement. scHiC-Diff employs a forward process that progressively perturbs contact maps and a reverse denoising process that reconstructs chromatin interactions from noisy observations. To better capture long-range dependencies in complex 3D genome structures, scHi-C contact matrices are treated as masked images and modeled using a Diffusion Transformer (DiT). Across two complementary simulated datasets and three real scHi-C datasets, scHiC-Diff improves the recovery of chromatin interaction patterns and enhances downstream analyses compared with existing methods. Application to a developmental scHi-C dataset further demonstrates improved reconstruction of chromatin organization and enhanced chromatin loop detection.

title: Latent effector capacity governs reversible T cell exhaustion: A theoretical mathematical model of PD-1 blockade response.
authors: Liew, Aubrey Y; Li, Ying; Dong, Haidong
abstract: T cell exhaustion is often viewed as a terminal state marked by irreversible loss of function during chronic infection and cancer. However, the rapid recovery of antitumor activity in clinical responders after PD-1 blockade suggests that some exhausted T cells retain hidden functional potential. To explain this paradox, we present a theoretical framework that separates latent effector capacity from active effector function. Latent effector capacity represents a history-dependent state reflecting preserved epigenetic accessibility and regulatory readiness, distinct from ongoing gene expression. In this model, PD-1 signaling acts as a reversible mask that suppresses effector function without eliminating the underlying effector capacity. The framework explains preserved chromatin accessibility, rapid reinvigoration after checkpoint blockade, and variable therapeutic responses. By incorporating nonlinear maintenance and erosion of latent effector capacity, the model predicts a bistable system with a point of no return beyond which exhaustion becomes irreversible. These principles may guide development of mechanistically informed biomarkers and artificial intelligence models predicting response to PD-1 therapy.

title: DESIGN: a framework for generative AI-enabled crop molecular design-driven breeding.
authors: Xu, Feng; Fu, Ran; Cheng, Qian; Jiang, Shuqin; Yan, Jun; Wang, Xiangfeng
abstract: Crop breeding is shifting from selecting naturally occurring variants to actively designing genetic features. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) provides a computational foundation for this transition; however, its application in crop systems remains limited. This review bridges this gap by systematically evaluating the translational potential of GenAI for crop molecular design breeding. We examine four major computational architectures and their applications across six key areas relevant to crop breeding: gene regulatory element design, protein engineering, small-molecule generation, gene-editing tool optimization, single-cell modeling, and cross-domain knowledge integration. Building on these advances, we propose the DESIGN framework, which organizes GenAI-enabled breeding into six synergistic capabilities: Discover, Engineer, Simulate, Integrate, Generate, and Navigate, thereby forming a closed-loop system spanning molecular design to field deployment. Finally, we discuss key bottlenecks in data, models, and validation, and outline a roadmap for translating GenAI into breeding practice. This review provides a conceptual and methodological foundation for the emerging paradigm of design-driven crop breeding.

title: Advances and Applications of Genome Editing in Precision Crop Breeding.
authors: Zhao, Jing; Qian, Xueyan; Zhong, Xiaofang; Xun, Hongwei; Guo, Dongquan
abstract: Genome editing is becoming an important tool for crop improvement by enabling precise modification of genetic variation. CRISPR-Cas technologies have expanded beyond nuclease-induced mutations to include base and prime editing, transcriptional and epigenetic regulation, multiplex editing, organelle editing and targeted DNA insertion. These advances support the development of agronomically valuable alleles and extend crop improvement beyond conventional selection, recombination and random mutagenesis. Applications now include plant architecture, yield-related traits, resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses, seed composition and nutritional quality, and extend to de novo domestication, haploid induction and hybrid breeding. Current research is increasingly moving from single-gene modification toward the engineering of promoters, cis-regulatory elements, quantitative alleles and multiple-gene editing, particularly in polyploid crops. Wider breeding applications will depend on efficient delivery and regeneration, recovery of transgene-free and heritable edited germplasm, reliable targeted insertion and validation across relevant environments. Integration with pangenomics, multi-omics, phenomics, artificial intelligence and predictive breeding may further improve target identification, allele design and prediction of editing outcomes, thereby supporting the development of more precise and efficient crop-breeding strategies.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Plant Gene Regulatory Networks.
authors: Yu, Haopeng
abstract: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are the maps that plant biologists most want to draw, with arrows pointing from transcription factors to the genes they control, explaining how plants develop and respond to the environment. Since experimental validation of even one arrow can take years, and a single plant genome harbours tens of millions of candidate TF-target pairs, this gap has driven the development of numerous computational methods for GRN inference. Here I review three generations of computational approaches to plant GRN inference and measure them against a five-level ladder of evidence, including statistical association, conditional dependence, physical binding, functional regulation and causal circuits. Classical statistics and machine learning have simplified complex gene expression data into clear, prioritised predictions. Techniques like single-cell and multi-omics methods help uncover cell type-specific networks based on chromatin accessibility and binding motifs. Now, deep learning can interpret cis-regulatory grammar directly from genome sequences, and foundation models trained on plant genomes and millions of cells hold exciting potential to share regulatory insights across different species. The most promising route forward is a lab-in-the-loop division of labour in which foundation models serve not as oracles but as hypothesis engines, collapsing fifty million candidate TF-target pairs into the few hundred edges most worth the bench's time, with each round of validation sharpening the next round of prediction.

title: Green Extraction and Molecular Docking-Guided Discovery of Asiaticoside as a Multi-Target Modulator of the SIRT1/HMGB1/p53-p21 Axis in H(2)O(2)-Induced Senescent Endothelial Cells.
authors: Li, Wenkai; Huang, Jianhua; Zeng, Fei; Wang, Yuping; Liu, Xiong; Wang, Junjie; Liu, Siyu
abstract: Endothelial cell senescence is a key contributor to vascular ageing and cardiovascular diseases. Asiaticoside, a pentacyclic triterpenoid saponin from Centella asiatica, exhibits anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities, yet its potential to modulate endothelial senescence remains unexplored. Herein, we report the molecular docking-guided discovery of asiaticoside as a multi-target modulator of the SIRT1/HMGB1/p53-p21 senescence regulatory axis. Asiaticoside was isolated via a green acid-hydrolysis strategy using dilute HCl as the extraction solvent, followed by polyamide enrichment and C(18) reversed-phase purification (purity > 98%). Molecular docking revealed that asiaticoside binds favourably to SIRT1 (-8.1 kcal mol(-1)), the HMGB1-DNA complex (-10.7 kcal mol(-1)), and several senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)-related inflammatory cytokines. In H(2)O(2)-induced senescent human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), asiaticoside at 100 muM significantly reduced senescence-associated beta-galactosidase activity and alleviated G0/G1 cell cycle arrest without cytotoxicity. Mechanistically, asiaticoside restored SIRT1 expression, suppressed the secretion of IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, and HMGB1, downregulated p21 at both mRNA and protein levels, reduced p53 protein expression, and suppressed p16 mRNA expression. These findings demonstrate that asiaticoside attenuates endothelial senescence and SASP-driven inflammation, an effect associated with restoration of SIRT1 expression and suppression of the HMGB1/p53-p21 pathway.

title: Design, Synthesis and Antitumor Activity Evaluation of Novel Dual G9a/EZH2 Inhibitors.
authors: Shi, Yajie; Zhang, Qiuyue; Zhang, Maoying; Zhao, Xiujuan; Zhang, Shuhang; Li, Jirui; Li, Haofeng; Fu, Chenglin; Chen, Guoliang
abstract: Targeting the crosstalk between histone methyltransferases G9a and EZH2 represents a promising strategy for cancer therapy. To improve upon our previously reported dual inhibitor SU08, we rationally designed and synthesized five series (SU, UA, UB, N, and L) of novel G9a/EZH2 dual inhibitors, incorporating diverse pyridone, urea, and thienopyrimidine moieties, yielding a total of 43 compounds. In vitro enzymatic screening revealed that compound SU101 against both EZH2 (IC(50) = 4.08 nM) and G9a (IC(50) = 2.92 nM) was comparable to SU08. Western blot analysis confirmed that SU101 and SU103 effectively suppressed both H3K27me3 and H3K9me2 expression in rhabdomyosarcoma RD cells. In cellular antiproliferative assays, SU101 showed the strongest activity (IC(50) = 15.33 muM). Molecular docking and dynamics simulations verified stable binding interactions between SU101 and both target proteins. Pharmacokinetic studies in rats demonstrated that SU101 possesses excellent oral bioavailability (94.3%), moderate plasma protein binding (84.6%), and an acceptable acute toxicity profile (LD(50) = 31.02 mg/kg in mice). Overall, these results suggest that SU101 may serve as a promising lead compound for further optimization and support the continued exploration of dual G9a/EZH2 inhibitors as a potential therapeutic approach for rhabdomyosarcoma.

title: Deep Learning and Domain Expertise for Fabricating High-Performance Biosensors.
authors: Xiao, Mei-Ling; Zhang, Pengcheng; Li, Zhijie; Lin, Nuo-Qiao; Wang, Xiaowo; Liu, Jian-Zhong
abstract: Transcription factor-based biosensors are essential for the scalable bioproduction of plant natural products. However, a major bottleneck in developing high-performance biosensors is the engineering of responsive promoters due to the vast sequence space and poorly understood sequence-function relationships. Here, we extend our previously published DeepSEED framework into an artificial intelligence-driven pipeline for efficient and extensible biosensor-responsive promoter optimization. This strategy integrates deep learning with domain-specific biological expertise. By fixing core promoter elements, varying the number and position of transcription factor binding sites (TFBSs) to define promoter backbones, and subsequently optimizing the flanking sequences, we enable the de novo design of promoters. We systematically apply this strategy to optimize a panel of biosensors across different transcription factors and regulatory modes, including four metabolite-responsive biosensors and a quorum-sensing-based environmental sensor. The resulting biosensors exhibit diverse dynamic behaviors with markedly improved sensitivity, expanded dynamic range, and increased maximum output. For instance, the optimized naringenin biosensor demonstrates a 32-fold broader dynamic range and a 27-fold higher maximum output compared to its parent. To illustrate its utility in metabolic engineering, we employed a DeepSEED-designed promoter to dynamically regulate a p-coumaric acid biosynthesis pathway, boosting production by 117.0%. Our work extends the previously published DeepSEED framework into a powerful pipeline for biosensor optimization and delivers a portfolio of high-performance regulatory elements, addressing a critical need and facilitating the development of more intelligent and productive metabolic engineering systems.

title: Integration by parts: The multi-layered mechanisms of cis-regulatory control.
authors: Cornwall-Scoones, Jake; Briscoe, James; Delas, M Joaquina
abstract: Cis-regulatory elements (CREs) integrate signals from transcription factors (TFs) to control gene expression, yet mechanisms underlying this information processing remain poorly understood. Deep learning demonstrates expression is predictable from CRE sequence, suggesting that unifying principles of regulation are within reach. Here, we propose a framework dividing CRE regulatory logic into two layers: binding-level integration, where cooperative TF interactions modulate DNA occupancy; and transcriptional-level integration, where TF effector domains and cofactors convert binding configurations into expression. At the binding level, we classify TF cooperativity along orthogonal axes-specific versus general, and symmetric versus asymmetric-encompassing protein-protein interactions, nucleosome competition, pioneer activity, and assisted loading. At the transcriptional level, cofactor interactions generate additive, synergistic, or antagonistic logic. Emerging from this complexity is a recurring quantitative pattern: "multiplication plus saturation," reconciling binding specificity with flexibility, explaining how short DNA motifs generate precise expression while maintaining evolvability, and informing synthetic biology and therapeutic applications.

title: Emerging frontiers for AI in single-cell genomics.
authors: Mitra, Sneha; Li, Jiaxin; Leslie, Christina S
abstract: We are just over a decade into the single-cell revolution in biology, which has been coupled to the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in single-cell genomics. Most early single-cell RNA embedding models and subsequent "foundation models"-representational models pretrained on large single-cell datasets-did not gain wide traction among experimental biologists. However, as massive single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) atlas efforts ramp up, there is a clear rationale for exploiting AI models to interpret new datasets in the context of vast existing data resources. Meanwhile, the advent of single-cell epigenetic/multiomic assays and Perturb-seq technologies presents new opportunities for AI modeling. Here, we review AI embedding and foundation models for scRNA-seq and single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (scATAC-seq), extensive machine-learning efforts to exploit single-cell multiome in regulatory genomics, and AI strategies to learn "virtual cell" models from Perturb-seq, ending with a description of current limitations of single-cell AI models and an outlook for future advances.

title: Recent advances in coarse-grained simulations of nucleic acid condensation.
authors: Fong Ng, Jessica; Li, Shanlong; Chen, Jianhan
abstract: Biomolecular condensates, formed through phase separation of multivalent biomolecules, play essential roles in cellular processes such as stress response, RNA processing, transcriptional control, and genome organization. Nucleic acids are increasingly recognized as important drivers and regulators of condensate formation and dynamics. This review examines recent advances in coarse-grained molecular simulations of dynamic nucleic acids and their phase transitions. We survey established computational frameworks validated against experimental data and discuss emerging applications that address increasingly complex systems. Existing studies reveal that base-mediated interactions emerge as dominant drivers in homotypic nucleic acid condensation and that simulation resolution fundamentally determines which physical phenomena are accessible and observable. We underscore that different modeling approaches at various resolutions provide complementary insights into nucleic acid condensation mechanisms and the driving forces. We emphasize the opportunities and challenges in extending these frameworks to capture the complexity of nucleic acid-mediated phase separation in biological contexts, while identifying important gaps in current modeling capabilities. Overall, molecular simulations at multiple scales have proven to be powerful tools for elucidating the mechanistic principles underlying nucleic acid condensates and their cellular functions.

title: Integrated multi-omics and genome mining strategies for activating cryptic polyketide biosynthetic gene clusters in Streptomyces: an overview.
authors: Santhoshkumar, R; Mohamed, Hafid; Jemo, Martin
abstract: Beneficial microbes from soil or marine habitats are promising sources for discovery of new bioactive compounds for medicine and agriculture, largely through biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) that encode the production of complex natural products for drug and antibiotic discovery. However, most BGCs are transcriptionally silent under standard testing conditions and may require a complex, integrated approach for activation. In this review, we revisit previous approaches to activating BGCs, focusing on polyketides. We additionally discuss how integrating genome mining strategies with multi-omics integration, synthetic biology methods, and precise genome-editing tools is providing increasingly precise strategies for the discovery and engineering of polyketide-producing Streptomyces. We further discuss how to couple artificial intelligence (AI)-designed promoters could enable the production of novel compounds with improved yields, expanded chemical diversity, and enhanced industrial potential. We further examine how state-of-the-art CRISPR-Cas systems, including base editing, facilitate precise editing of high-GC-content genomes while circumventing the genome instability and Cas9-associated cellular toxicity that frequently accompany double-strand break formation in Streptomyces, and how chromatin topology rewiring dismantles transcriptional silencing. Unlike reviews that address genome mining, pathway engineering, or genome editing as separate approaches, this review presents an integrated framework linking computational BGC prediction, multi-omics validation, and precision engineering to prioritize and activate cryptic polyketide pathways in Streptomyces. We propose comprehensive computational genomics prediction approaches and integrate them with experimental validation through promoter engineering, transcription factor decoys, and chassis strain optimization, highlighting how these methods and tools are advancing the field from descriptive BGC catalogs to scalable, predictive models for next-generation drug discovery. Future efforts to couple AI-generated, sequence-orthogonal promoter libraries with biology-based modeling hold great promise.

title: A microexon regulatory code reveals autism-linked genetic variation.
authors: Parada, Guillermo E; Bretschneider, Hannes; Li, Jack Daiyang; Fine, Jacob L; Dupas, Steven J; Ellis, Jonathan D; Braunschweig, Ulrich; Bonnal, Sophie; Dalal, Taykhoom; Engchuan, Worrawat; Zarrei, Mehdi; Wei, Wei; Zafar, Nadia; Hemberg, Martin; Attisano, Liliana; Ellis, James; Irimia, Manuel; Wainberg, Michael; Trost, Brett; Scherer, Stephen W; Morris, Quaid D; Blencowe, Benjamin J
abstract: Neuronal microexons are a highly conserved class of alternative splicing events enriched in genes with critical functions in nervous system biology(1,2). Microexon splicing is often disrupted in the brains of autistic individuals, and mice with microexon deficiencies display autism-like phenotypes(1,3,4). However, the full landscape of microexons is not known, and the impact of genetic variation on these exons has not been systematically investigated. Here, through extensive transcriptome profiling, we detect hundreds of new microexons, including many with neuronal subtype-specific splicing patterns, and others that activate nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Using machine learning, we define a sequence code predictive of neuronally spliced microexons and use this to identify critical regulatory elements surrounding the expanded microexon repertoire. This code further reveals genomic variants predicted to alter microexon splicing in individuals affected by autism, with rare variants having the strongest estimated impact. These variants are mostly detected in idiopathic individuals and are associated with autism status. They also converge on synaptic and other autism-linked genes, as well as genes not previously linked to autism. Our results collectively define an expanded repertoire of microexons, delineate their regulatory code, and pinpoint variants predicted to affect their splicing, with implications for the disruption of functions central to neuronal biology and brain disorders.

title: Molecular dynamics guided all-atom reconstruction of cryo-ET maps reveals mechanisms of histone tail mediated chromatin compaction.
authors: Li, Shuxiang; Aristizabal, Maria J; Grigoryev, Sergei A; Panchenko, Anna R
abstract: Dynamics and physical state of chromatin are crucial in regulating gene expression, DNA replication, and repair. Intrinsically disordered histone tails were previously recognized as key modulators of chromatin states. However, detailed atomistic mechanisms by which histone tail dynamics are associated with chromatin compaction and higher-order chromatin organization remain poorly understood. In this work, we combine extensive all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of tri-nucleosomes with varying linker lengths and cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) of native nucleosome arrays. Our approach offers distinct advantages as it elucidates realistic inter-nucleosomal interactions and tri-nucleosome orientations derived from physics-based MD simulations, enabling a more accurate and physically grounded interpretation of cryo-ET data. The results reveal that tri-nucleosome models can be successfully used for fitting and the near-atomistic interpretation of cryo-ET density maps of native human chromatin. Moreover, histone tails were shown to promote chromatin compaction via three major patterns: through histone-DNA interactions, histone H2A-H4 and H3-H4 tail-tail interactions. Notably, the distributions of MD-generated structural parameters of tri-nucleosomes were found to be in strong agreement with those of experimental condensed chromatin arrays.

title: Quantifying the impact of genetic mutations on enhancer dynamics.
authors: Das, Maitreya; Banerjee, Deepro; Hossain, Ayaan; Jensen, Matthew; Mogre, Saie; Sun, Jiawan; Mao, Joseph; Glick, Adam B; Salis, Howard M; Girirajan, Santhosh
abstract: Transcriptional regulation is mediated by enhancers, yet how genetic perturbations alter enhancer activity and gene expression remains unclear. We develop UDI-UMI-STARR-seq, integrating dual indexes and unique molecular identifiers, and combine it with RNA-seq to profile perturbation-associated changes in enhancer activity and gene expression. We apply this approach to 253,632 fragments representing 46,142 cell type-specific candidate enhancers and assess the impact of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of six transcription factors (ATF2, CTCF, FOXA1, LEF1, TCF7L2, and SCRT1). We identify responsive fragments that are repressed or induced and enriched for p53 family motifs. Enhancer-gene mapping reveals associations between responsive fragments and gene expression changes, including Wnt/p53 targets after ATF2 or LEF1 depletion. A deep learning model recapitulates enhancer grammar, including cooperative motif syntax and flanking sequence context. Applying this framework to 16p12.1 deletion identifies responsive fragments associated with genes involved in neuronal function, providing a scalable readout of enhancer dynamics across genetic perturbations.

title: Advances in plant metabolic engineering through synthetic biology.
authors: Alsuwat, Hind; Alvarez, Derry; Al-Babili, Salim
abstract: The challenges associated with the escalating global population and climate change in crop production and food security are substantial. This underscores the necessity for improvements in crop nutrition, yield, and resilience to environmental stresses. Plant metabolic pathways directly influence growth, nutrient accumulation, and stress responses, rendering them prime targets for crop enhancement. Advances in plant synthetic biology and gene editing are facilitating more precise modifications of genes, regulatory elements, and metabolic pathways. This review highlights the primary technologies used in plant metabolic engineering and focuses on representative examples of their implementation for crop improvement, including but not limited to CRISPR-Cas systems, multiplex genome editing, knock-in and knock-out strategies, CRISPR-mediated gene regulation (CRISPRi/CRISPRa), base editing, prime editing, RNA targeting technologies, synthetic promoters, and gene stacking strategies. Furthermore, the emerging role of artificial intelligence in the design and optimization of metabolic pathways and genome editing tools will be briefly discussed.

title: Transcription factor CTCF activates KIAA1199 expression to inhibit ferroptosis and promote malignant behaviors in colorectal cancer based on bioinformatics and machine learning.
authors: Fan, Xiaoye; Meng, Lei; Zheng, Song; He, Xiaoqing
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a common malignancy of the colon and rectum, but its molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. METHODS: Gene expression omnibus (GEO) database was used to download CRC-related datasets. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), support vector machine (SVM), and random forest (RF) were used to identify key CRC genes. Cell type identification by estimating relative subsets of rna transcripts (CIBERSORT) was used for immune infiltration analysis. Tumor immune estimation resource (TIMER) database was used to assess gene expression across multiple cancers. Human transcription factor target database (hTFtarget) was used to predict regulatory relationships between genes and transcription factors. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), dual-luciferase assay, cell transfection, western blot (WB), and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) were used to detect protein-gene binding, transcriptional activity, gene knockdown and overexpression, protein expression, and mRNA expression. JASPAR database was used to identify transcription factor binding sites. Cells were treated with a BODIPY 581/591 C11 kit to assess intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. The assay kits were employed to determine the levels of ferrous iron (Fe(2+)), malondialdehyde (MDA), and superoxide dismutase (SOD). Cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) was performed to measure cell viability. RESULTS: Matrix metallopeptidase 7 (MMP7), KIAA1199, and cadherin 3 (CDH3) were identified as potential key CRC genes. Their expression correlated with altered immune cell infiltration patterns. KIAA1199 showed the highest upregulation in CRC tissues. CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) transcriptionally activated KIAA1199. Knockdown of CTCF decreased the expression of solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), while increasing ROS, Fe(2+), and MDA, and decreasing SOD levels. CTCF knockdown combined with KIAA1199 overexpression partially rescued these effects, modulating ferroptosis-related oxidative stress in CRC cells. CONCLUSION: CTCF transcriptionally activates KIAA1199 and regulates ferroptosis-related oxidative stress in CRC cells, providing new insights into the molecular mechanisms of CRC.

title: Regional Adipose Distribution Reveals Differential Genetic Risk Patterns for Cardiometabolic Diseases.
authors: Wu, Qian; Yang, Fan; An, Qi; Liu, Ying; Tian, Hexian; Du, Yamin; Cai, Wenjie; Lei, Minghuan; Xu, Jinglei; Deng, Linlin; Zhai, Ying; Zhang, Zhihui; Wu, Yue; Wang, Haolin; Cheng, Yue; Liu, Feng; Li, Dong
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cardiometabolic risk associated with obesity is increasingly recognized to be strongly influenced by the anatomical distribution and ectopic deposition of adipose tissue, yet the genetic mechanisms linking adipose depots to cardiometabolic diseases remain incompletely understood. METHODS: Using large-scale genome-wide association summary statistics, we systematically characterized shared genetic architecture between 7 magnetic resonance imaging-derived regional and ectopic adipose traits and 20 cardiometabolic diseases, including major cardiovascular outcomes and type 2 diabetes. Genetic overlap was assessed at genome-wide, regional, and variant levels, followed by functional annotation, cell-type enrichment, and phenotype enrichment analyses. Protein-protein interaction networks and molecular docking analyses were further applied to prioritize disease-relevant genes and potential therapeutic compounds. RESULTS: We identified widespread yet heterogeneous genetic overlap, including 109 adipose-cardiometabolic diseases pairs with genome-wide overlap, 92 pairs showing regional concordance across 423 genomic regions, and 146 pleiotropic loci supported by colocalization. Shared variants were enriched in regulatory elements and connected to pleiotropic genes involved in metabolic and inflammatory pathways, including insulin signaling, ion homeostasis, and cellular stress responses. Cell type enrichment analyses highlighted immune, endothelial, and metabolically active parenchymal cells as key contributing cell types. Network and docking analyses further prioritized cardiometabolic disease-related genes such as MMP9, PPARG, and TM6SF2, along with candidate compounds exhibiting favorable binding properties. CONCLUSIONS: This study delineates differential genetic risk patterns linking adipose distribution to multiple cardiometabolic diseases and reveals interconnected metabolic, immune, and vascular mechanisms, providing a genetic framework for cardiometabolic and cardiovascular risk assessment and the prioritization of potential therapeutic targets.

title: Central Dogma Transformer II: an AI microscope for understanding cellular regulatory mechanisms.
authors: Ota, Nobuyuki
abstract: MOTIVATION: Interpretability is not optional in biology: understanding gene regulation requires models whose learned structure can be directly interrogated, not merely accurate predictors whose internals resist mapping onto regulatory relationships. We ask whether an architecture mirroring the central dogma yields attention and gradient maps that recover known regulatory elements and networks in inspectable form. RESULTS: Central Dogma Transformer II (CDT-II) mirrors the central dogma in its architecture-DNA self-attention, RNA self-attention, and DNA-to-RNA cross-attention-requiring only genomic embeddings and raw per-cell expression. On K562 CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) data with five genes held out entirely, CDT-II predicts perturbation effects (per-gene mean r = 0.84 ), recovers the GFI1B regulatory network (6.6-fold enrichment, P = 3.5 x 10-17 ), and concentrates cross-attention on ENCODE regulatory elements including CTCF sites (mean 7.67  x  across 28 target genes, P < .001 ). Gradient attribution predicts consequences of perturbing therapeutic targets (mean r = 0.82 ). For TFRC, target of the anti-TfR1 antibody PPMX-T003, it identifies erythrocyte-structure, iron-dependent DNA-synthesis and oxidative-stress genes, matching anemia and ferroptosis reported clinically and preclinically-without clinical data as input. CDT-II acts as an AI microscope, surfacing clinically relevant regulatory structure from perturbation experiments alone. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Source code is available at https://github.com/nobusama/CDT2. Pre-computed embeddings, training data, and model weights are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/nobusama17/CDT2-data.

title: Genetic risk and inflammatory signaling converge on cell type-specific regulatory programs in type 1 diabetes.
authors: Wang, Liu; Wei, Zong
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a complex autoimmune disease characterized by the destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells. Both genetic susceptibility and epigenetic dysregulation contribute to T1D risk. Recent studies have reported beta-cell dysfunction before disease onset, suggesting that beta-cell-intrinsic mechanisms contribute to pathogenesis. However, the mechanistic link between disease-associated variants and beta-cell dysfunction remains poorly understood. We hypothesized that a subset of T1D-associated variants directly influences cell type-specific candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) by disrupting transcription factor (TF) binding and altering gene expression. To define cell type-specific cCREs in human islets, we integrated publicly available epigenomic datasets, including bulk histone modification profiles and single-cell multiomic data from human pancreatic islets. We combined these data with T1D genome-wide association study (GWAS) variants to identify disease-associated SNPs located within enhancer regions. Using multiomic datasets from PANC-DB, we characterized cell type-specific chromatin accessibility in nondiabetic and T1D islets and identified regulatory regions that may control gene expression in beta cells and other islet cell types. We then applied ChromBPNet, a deep learning model that predicts base-pair-resolution chromatin accessibility from scATAC-seq data, to evaluate how specific variants may alter local regulatory activity. In parallel, we used TF footprinting to nominate TFs likely to bind these variant-containing regions. These analyses identified several T1D-associated SNPs predicted to alter chromatin accessibility at candidate TF binding sites, suggesting mechanisms by which noncoding variants may contribute to beta-cell dysfunction and T1D susceptibility. Our findings link T1D-associated variants to cell type-specific enhancer activity and regulatory pathways and provide candidates for future mechanistic studies.

title: CRISCross: Integration of Epigenetic Information for Deep-Learning-Based Prediction of CRISPR-Cas9 Off-Targets Across Cell Types
authors: Pargeter WJ; Rabsch D; Kaufmann MM; Uhl M; Mitrofanov A; Brox T; Cathomen T; Tran VD; Backofen R
abstract:
CRISPR-Cas9 enables precise genome editing but remains limited by off-target effects, raising safety concerns and necessitating accurate prediction. Although epigenetic features influence Cas9 binding and cleavage, their predictive signals are often weak, highly variable, and context-dependent, limiting the effectiveness of existing machine learning approaches. Cross-cell-type settings are especially challenging: epigenetic landscapes differ substantially, and models trained on one cell type frequently fail to generalize. Here, we systematically investigate the role of epigenetic context in off-target prediction and demonstrate that its utility depends on modeling interactions with sequence features rather than treating it as an independent signal. Tabular and deep learning experiments demonstrate that epigenetic features provide a consistent but modestly complementary signal, and that late-stage fusion strategies are insufficient to effectively exploit this information. To address this, we introduce CRISCross, a cross-attention-based architecture that captures sequence-epigenetic interactions at the nucleotide level, alongside CRISPRAT, a synthetic pretraining strategy that learns transferable representations from genome-derived sgRNA-off-target pairs without relying on dataset-specific pretraining. CRISCross, incorporating AlphaGenome-derived chromatin accessibility signals, shows better predictive performance than sequence-only baselines across three independent test datasets spanning two cell types, demonstrating improved generalization across guide RNAs, datasets, and cellular contexts. This is particularly relevant for therapeutic applications involving cell types or patient-derived contexts that lack dedicated experimental datasets. In such settings, predicted chromatin accessibility may provide scalable contextual information when direct epigenomic profiling is unavailable or impractical. Together, these results show that accurate CRISPR off-target prediction benefits from interaction-aware integration of epigenetic context alongside generalizable pretraining strategies.

title: DNA-LLM2Vec: Architecture-Aware Task-Conditioned Adaptation of Decoder DNA Foundation Models
authors: Liang Y; Zhai K; Gan Y; Li S; Shao J; Watson GH; Poesio M
abstract: Decoder DNA foundation models pretrain with dense next-token prediction and scale to long sequences, but their representations are directional. This is a poor fit for genomic tasks that need sequence context both upstream and downstream of a locus. Bidirectional masked-language-model encoders supply this context, but they pretrain more sparsely and scale less easily to long windows. We introduce DNA-LLM2Vec, a staged decoder-to-encoder framework that opens bidirectional context, repairs the resulting mismatch with masked next-token prediction, and applies contrastive views encoding strand and positional invariance. We instantiate it on two architecturally distinct backbones, DNAGPT and HyenaDNA, and evaluate seven biological task families (grouped from GB, NT, GUE, and GUE+EPI) with frozen linear probing. The benefits of conversion are architecture-aware and task-conditioned rather than uniform. Crop-based positional contrastive learning helps most for the extended-context families (enhancer-promoter interaction and Virus-COVID), raising frozen Avg-EPI MCC to 27.5% for DNAGPT and 26.7% for HyenaDNA, whereas for shorter, local families the results depend on backbone and tokenisation. Beyond classification, bidirectional context and MNTP improve causal-eQTL variant-effect prediction specifically at distance, and a base-pair mutagenesis diagnostic shows that adaptation organises motif-aware contact structure while reverse-complement training imprints strand-consistent geometry, yet neither predicts the best downstream view. DNA-LLM2Vec therefore produces frozen bidirectional representations whose most effective adaptation view depends on the task structure and the backbone. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/semi-nothing/dna-llm2vec.

title: A relational architecture of the human genome
authors: Krause J; Danner M; Kraft F; Islam T; Begemann M; Ziad Z; Elbracht M; Bode M; Kurth I
abstract: Complex systems exhibit organization not only through their components but also via their interdependencies. Local nucleotide dependencies underpin regulatory motifs and RNA structures, yet principles governing a higher-order organization across the human genome remain unknown. Here we systematically perturbed every position of the com- plete telomere-to-telomere human genome using Nucleotide Transformer v3 with an ex- ascale compute cluster, generating nucleotide-resolution dependency maps that reveal a directed, weighted network of position-to-position genomic relationships. This network recapitulates known biological features and uncovers recurrent, directional architec- tures termed 'relons', spanning coding, non-coding, and unannotated regions. These re- lational modules reflect evolutionary and functional constraints and associate with hu- man genetic variation and pathogenic variants. Our findings suggest a higher-order rela- tional layer of genome organization, providing a framework to interpret DNA as a complex system of dependencies beyond linear and 3D structure, with implications for under- standing genetic variation and disease.

title: A high-resolution protein-RNA binding atlas for structure-aware interaction prediction and post-transcriptional regulatory modeling
authors: Karimzadeh M; Fish L; Karner H; Linder J; Emadi A; Hernandez-Corchado A; Smaili FZ; Stewart EM; Kelley DR; Wang B; Najafabadi HS; Leonetti M; Goodarzi H
abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) control post-transcriptional gene expression by regulating RNA processing, localization, stability, and translation. However, our understanding of RNA regulation remains limited by the resolution, scale, and uniformity of available RBP binding maps. Here we introduce eclair CLIP (ecCLIP), a high-throughput CLIP-seq platform that combines endogenous protein tagging for uniform affinity capture with ligation-free library preparation to generate high-resolution RNA-protein binding profiles. We applied ecCLIP to 67 endogenously tagged RBPs in HEK293T cells, generating a high-quality transcriptome-scale atlas that recovered known binding preferences and captured post-transcriptional regulons linked to RNA half-life. To test the utility of the atlas, we incorporated ecCLIP into Borzuki, a Borzoi-derived sequence-to-function model trained on complementary RNA degradation, expression, CLIP, and Perturb-seq data. Inclusion of ecCLIP data improved RNA half-life prediction and assessment of 3′ UTR variant effects on RNA stability, demonstrating that our atlas helps capture RNA dynamics. To directly model the cis-regulatory grammar underlying these RBP-RNA interactions, we developed Pythia, a structure-aware neural network architecture that incorporates context-free grammar-inspired fixed convolutions to explicitly encode RNA base-pairing features. Pythia predicted RBP binding from sequence and structural context and decomposed predictions into sequence- and structure-dependent components. We tested this decomposition for five RBPs using massively parallel reporter CLIP (MPRC) binding assays in cells, using synthetic RNA libraries containing mutations designed to preserve or disrupt predicted RNA structures across nominated binding sites. We used the same MPRC strategy to confirm allele-specific binding effects for variants prioritized by Pythia. Together, ecCLIP and Pythia provide a resource for structure-aware decoding of RNA-protein interaction grammar and interpretation of post-transcriptional regulatory variation.
